### Page note: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/brain-aneurysm/symptoms-causes/syc-20361483
Stored documents: doc-c374dddd1acb
Reader state: complete; relevance: partial
**Page:** Brain aneurysm – Symptoms & causes – Mayo Clinic  
URL: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/brain-aneurysm/symptoms-causes/syc-20361483  

**Evidence**  

| Risk Factor | Source quote |
|-------------|--------------|
| **Age** (30‑60 years) | “Brain aneurysms can happen at any age. **However, they’re more common in adults between ages 30 and 60**.” |
| **Female sex** | “Brain aneurysms are more common in women than in men.” |
| **Cigarette smoking** | “Cigarette smoking. **Smoking is a risk factor for brain aneurysms to form and for brain aneurysms to rupture.**” |
| **High blood pressure** | “High blood pressure. **This condition can weaken arteries. Aneurysms are more likely to form and to rupture in weakened arteries.**” |
| **Drug use, especially cocaine** | “Drug use, particularly using cocaine. **Drug use raises blood pressure.** … may lead to an infection, which may cause an aneurysm.” |
| **Heavy alcohol use** | “Heavy alcohol use. **This also can increase blood pressure.**” |
| **Inherited connective tissue conditions (e.g., Ehlers–Danlos syndrome)** | “Inherited connective tissue conditions, **such as Ehlers‑Danlos syndrome.**” |
| **Polycystic kidney disease** | “Polycystic kidney disease. **This inherited condition results in fluid‑filled sacs in the kidneys. It also may increase blood pressure.**” |
| **Aortic coarctation (narrow aorta)** | “A narrow aorta, also called coarctation of the aorta.” |
| **Brain arteriovenous malformation (AVM)** | “Brain arteriovenous malformation, also called brain AVM.” |
| **Family history of brain aneurysm** | “A family history of brain aneurysm. **The risk is higher if you have family members who have had a brain aneurysm.**” |
| **Large aneurysm (for rupture)** | “Having a large aneurysm.” |
| **Certain aneurysm locations (for rupture)** | “Having aneurysms in certain locations.” |
| **Irregular aneurysm shape / daughter sac (for rupture)** | “Having an irregular shape of the aneurysm or having an outpouching on the aneurysm, called a daughter sac.” |
| **Uncontrolled high blood pressure (for rupture)** | “Having untreated high blood pressure.” |

*All quotes are from the “Risk factors” section of the page.*

**Missing**  
- Risk factors for an **abdominal aortic aneurysm** (no such list on this page).  
- Risk factors for a **thoracic aortic aneurysm** (no such list on this page).  
- No explicit comparison or statement indicating which risk factors are common to all three aneurysm types.

| Endovascular coiling | https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/brain-aneurysm/multimedia/aneurysm-coil/img-20007617 | Media page, not a risk‑factor list. |

query: Mayo Clinic thoracic aortic aneurysm risk factors
information:
### Page note: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/thoracic-aortic-aneurysm/symptoms-causes/syc-20350188
Stored documents: doc-af8d4bda4f3c
Reader state: complete; relevance: partial
**Page:** Thoracic aortic aneurysm – Symptoms and causes (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/thoracic-aortic-aneurysm/symptoms-causes/syc-20350188)

**Evidence**  
* **Risk factors** (Thoracic aortic aneurysm)  
  * **Age.**  “Thoracic aortic aneurysms occur most often in people age 65 and older.”【2, line 67】  
  * **Smoking and tobacco use.**  “If you smoke or chew tobacco, it's important that you quit. Using tobacco also can worsen an aneurysm and overall health.”【2, line 68】  
  * **High blood pressure.**  “Increased blood pressure damages the blood vessels in the body. This raises the risk of an aneurysm.”【2, line 69】  
  * **Coronary artery disease.**  “This type of heart disease causes reduced blood flow to the heart. It's often caused by atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis can damage the lining of a blood vessel, increasing the risk of an aneurysm.”【2, line 70】  
  * **Family history.**  “You're more likely to get an aortic aneurysm and rupture if you have a parent, brother, sister or child with one. You may develop aneurysms at a younger age.”【2, line 71】

* **Other related categories (listed under Causes or general discussion) that may serve as risk factors for aneurysms more broadly**  
  * **Atherosclerosis** – “A buildup of fats, cholesterol, and other substances in and on the artery walls causes the arteries to get stiff. Over time, the walls of the arteries may get weak.”【2, line 45】  
  * **Genetic conditions** – “Aortic aneurysms in younger people are often caused by changes in genes. A genetic condition called Marfan syndrome can weaken the wall of the aorta.”【2, line 47】  
  * **Blood vessel inflammation** – “Conditions that cause irritation and swelling of blood vessels, such as Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis, are associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms.”【2, line 53】  
  * **Bicuspid aortic valve** – “People who are born with a bicuspid valve are more likely to get a thoracic aneurysm.”【2, line 56】  
  * **Untreated infection** – “Though rare, it’s possible to get a thoracic aortic aneurysm if you’ve had an untreated infection such as syphilis or salmonella.”【2, line 58】  
  * **Traumatic injury** – “Some people who are injured in falls or motor vehicle crashes get thoracic aortic aneurysms. But this is rare.”【2, line 60】

* **Relationship to abdominal aortic aneurysm**  
  * “Thoracic aortic aneurysms are less common than aneurysms in the lower part of the aorta, called abdominal aortic aneurysms.”【2, line 64】

**Missing**  
* No risk‑factor list for **abdominal aortic aneurysm** or **brain aneurysm** is present on this page.  
* No explicit statement of any risk factor common to all three aneurysm types.  

**Next links**  
* Reference list entry **“Aortic aneurysm”** (source 1) – likely links to a general Mayo Clinic page that may contain risk‑factor information applicable to abdominal and brain aneurysms.  
* Menu link **“Diseases & Conditions”** → “Aortic aneurysm” – could lead to a page covering all aneurysm types and their shared risk factors.  
* The page contains links to “Diagnosis & treatment,” “Doctors & departments,” and “Care at Mayo Clinic,” which are not expected to contain risk‑factor lists.
